**Title:** MHD simulations on the large-scale propagation of high-speed solar wind streams
**Authors:** Stefan J. Hofmeister
**Date:** Submitted 2 May 2026 (arXiv:2605.01613, v1)
**Journal:** None listed. This is an arXiv preprint in astro-ph.SR, cross-listed to physics.plasm-ph.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim within the quoting limits, so here is a condensed paraphrase. The paper uses three-dimensional MHD simulations to follow high-speed streams from near the Sun to 1 AU. It tracks both global stream structure and individual plasma parcels. It finds that streams are not parcel-preserving, so peak velocity, density, and temperature can give misleading radial trends, and it proposes velocity-based relationships for linking parcels. Stream evolution is dominated by interaction regions, with fast-wind deceleration, slow-wind acceleration, and heating. A boundary layer near the Sun can dominate narrow streams. Latitudinal flows redistribute mass and flux and reduce center-to-flank contrast. Radial flux is conserved, but total field strength is not in spherical sampling. Observed properties and geoeffectiveness depend on sampling location, stream geometry, and latitudinal deflection. The full text is available at arxiv.org/abs/2605.01613.

**Does it describe the idealized setup and quantitative results?**

No, not based on the content provided. The abstract and page metadata don't specify the simulation setup parameters you listed (boundary speeds, density, temperature, B, inner radius, or tilt). The results are described qualitatively ("compression," "significant heating," "boundary layer"). No compression ratio or shock formation distance is given. Those details would likely be in the full PDF or HTML version, which I did not have.

2.2. The MULTI-VP model
The MULTI-VP model (Pinto & Rouillard 2017) is a coronal
model that solves a set of equations (eq. 6, 7, 8) to provide the
solar wind conditions at 0.1 AU (wind speed, density, tempera-
(bulk speed: Vb, proton density: n, temperature: T, interplane-
tary magnetic ﬁeld (IMF) φ-angle, magnitude of the IMF: B, the
three components of the IMF: Bx, By, Bz) of the studied HSSs
are presented as a function of time in GSE coordinates. The sim-
ulations were conducted by assuming a uniform mesh of 4◦in
longitude (90 cells), latitude (30 cells) and a radial resolution of
512 cells (radial step of ∆r ≈0.0037 AU). The boundary val-
ues at 0.1 AU are provided at the standard 2◦x 2◦resolution by
WSA∗, no matter the employed magnetogram. In the MULTI-
VP case, the boundary values are provided at 2◦x 2◦resolution
when employing a GONG magnetogram and at 5◦x 5◦when us-
ing WSO magnetograms, as described in Section 3. Figures 9,
11, 13, and 15 show the simulated solar wind radial velocity in
3D space, presented around the moment when the studied HSS
reached Earth.
5.1. HSS case during the period of low solar activity
In Fig. 8, we observe that both the bulk solar wind speed as
well as the proton density signatures at Earth are reproduced
by MULTI-VP+EUHFORIA-heliosphere (blue line) while this
is not the case for the WSA∗+EUHFORIA-heliosphere. More-
over, results with the former set-up show an increase in tempera-
ture above the slow solar wind levels by the time the HSS reaches
Earth. Although this increase does not reach the values observed
at L1 by the WIND spacecraft, it is closer to the observations
than the values obtained by WSA∗+EUHFORIA-heliosphere.
The IMF φ-angle is captured well by both models, but the po-
larity of MULTI-VP+EUHFORIA-heliosphere changes earlier.
Therefore, it is in better agreement with the observed polarity
change on late Jan. 18. The ﬂuctuations of the total magnetic
ﬁeld (B) as well as its Bx and By components at the stream
interaction, are better reproduced by MULTI-VP+EUHFORIA-
heliosphere. However, the models are not expected to reproduce
the ﬂuctuations of the IMF Bz component since the meridional
component of the magnetic ﬁeld is always set to zero at 0.1 AU.
This causes the models to severely underestimate Bz throughout
the simulation domain. In Fig. 9, we visualize the simulated ra-
dial velocity in 3D space. More speciﬁcally, Fig. 9a shows a HSS
arriving at Earth with velocities between [520, 600] km/s, while
in Fig. 9b, no HSS seems to impact the planet during the period
of interest.

The plasma number density of the fast solar wind at the same radius is nfsw = 300 cm−3, while sgn(Bcorona) is
the sign of the magnetic field as given by the coronal model. Also, the plasma thermal pressure is constant at the
boundary and equal to P = 3.3 nPa corresponding to a temperature of Tfsw = 0.8 MK in the fast solar wind (see
Pomoell & Poedts (2018) for more details). The parameter ρ denotes the mass density with ρfsw = 0.5nfswmp, where
mp is the proton mass.
Equation 1 is of utmost importance since it provides velocities at 0.1 au based on which all other plasma and magnetic
parameters are calculated. However, it is interesting to understand how this semi-empirical formula was first derived.
If we go back to the literature (Arge et al. 2003, 2004; van der Holst et al. 2010), we see that eq. 1 was formulated after
ballistically mapping the solar wind from L1 back to 0.1 au and searching for patterns between speeds and a number
of photospheric/coronal parameters. A large number of test functions and values of constants were tried in eq. 1 until
a good comparison with observations at 1 au was achieved, after propagating the WSA velocities ballistically to Earth
using a simple 1D kinematic model and a specific type of magnetograms (originally Mount Wilson Solar observatory
maps and more recently, GONG and VSM mpas). However, a kinematic model is different from an MHD polytropic
model (as EUHFORIA) in the following ways. First, the velocity of the solar wind in the kinematic model is radial
and does not change with distance except to conserve mass and mass flux at the stream interaction regions (Kim
et al. 2014). No acceleration of the solar wind takes place as it propagates outwards, only decelerations at the stream
interaction regions.
On the other hand, an MHD polytropic model accelerates the supersonic and super-Alvfenic
solar wind due to polytropic expansion and it takes into account much more complex stream interaction dynamics.
Therefore, it is apparent that eq. 1 does not seem to be consistent when used to produce boundary conditions for 3D
MHD polytropic models.
To account for this inconsistency, a number of ad hoc assumptions were adopted in EUHFORIA (and in other models
similar to it, such as Enlil, see McGregor et al. 2008; Owens et al. 2008, for more details). First, 50 km/s are subtracted
from the velocities at 0.1 au to account for the acceleration caused by the MHD heliospheric model when it propagates
velocities in the interplanetary space (Pomoell & Poedts 2018). Secondly, velocities at 0.1 au are capped between a
range, usually that is [275, 625] km/s. The reason of these constraints has not been clearly justified throughout the
literature. The main argument behind the upper limit, is that velocities above 625 km/s tend to overestimate the
fast solar wind at Earth. On the other hand, the reasoning behind the lower limit, is that velocities below 275 km/s
could be sub-Alfv´enic, something that it is not handled correctly by the MHD code. Even though these assumptions
help us reconstruct the large-scale structure of the solar wind at Earth, we often miss the precise prediction of e.g.,
well-defined high-speed streams (HSSs; see, for example, Hinterreiter et al. 2019; Samara et al. 2021). Moreover, the
dynamics between the slow and the fast solar wind are generally poorly reproduced (see e.g., Samara et al. 2022).
However, it will be unfair to claim that the not fully accurate performance of EUHFORIA (and similar models) is
solely caused because of this discrepancy. The problem of improving solar wind modeling is a multi-variable problem
that depends on a number of parameters, such as the magnetograms used, the kind of model used and assumptions

Our results show that the change in the modeling output at Earth based on the different γ is noticeable for the
temperature and mildly noticeable for velocity (Fig. 9a,b). This behaviour is expected, and can be predicted from the
analysis of the heliospheric part of Parker’s polytropic solar wind solutions. Figure 10a shows how the velocity varies
as a function of heliocentric distance for three synthetic solar wind stream cases with an initial velocity of 300, 500,
and 700 km/s at 0.1 au. Different colors correspond to different γ values. Figure 10b presents how the temperature
varies as a power law with heliocentric distance, for the same solar wind streams and γ values. When we change
the γ at 0.1 au we practically change the temperature slope. Therefore, at any heliocentric distance the temperature
will differ depending on the γ employed and the different slope that this change caused. However, this effect is only
slightly apparent for velocities. All curves after ≈0.25 au have very similar slopes. As we are varying γ only from
0.1 au upwards, the effect on the velocity is minimal because the flows are already well supersonic and approaching
their asymptotic values. The radial decay of temperature, on the other hand, depends directly on γ, and differences
can be significant at 1 au even for a modification of γ from 0.1 au upwards only. Therefore, adding more heating to
the system by lowering γ does not expect to lead to better velocity predictions at Earth.

6. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
In this study we investigated how the calibration of the WSA model, as implemented in EUHFORIA, can be
performed based on single-point PSP observations. We employed PSP data between 0.1 – 0.4 au from the first 8
encounters during the solar minimum period of solar cycle 24 – 25 so that the influence from solar transients is
minimal. We focused on the calibration of four constants in the WSA relationship shown in eq. 1, namely, those that
could be fine-tuned based on observations and past studies according to the methodology of McGregor et al. (2011).
These are the parameters V0 and V1, which correspond to the lowest velocity observed at the heliocentric distance of
interest, and the maximum velocity range that solar wind can vary above V0. Also, the parameter w which indicates
the angular distance from the CH boundary at which the transition from slow to fast solar wind takes place, and the
parameter β which shows how abrupt this transition is.
Calibrating the WSA model at 0.1 au based on PSP observations did not lead to better predictions at Earth.
